title: Displacement Current
short_intro: Displacement current is a quantity appearing in Maxwell's equations that is defined in terms of the rate of change of electric displacement field or electric flux. It was introduced by James Clerk Maxwell to resolve the inconsistency in Ampere's Circuital Law for non-steady currents.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of displacement current, relation with changing electric flux, identification in charging capacitors, and modification of Ampere's law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of Maxwell's modified curl equation for magnetic field, symmetry of Maxwell's equations, magnetic field between capacitor plates, and wave equation for electromagnetic waves in free space.

concept_notes.heading: Failure of Original Ampere's Law
bullets: Ampere's Circuital Law states that the line integral of magnetic field B along a closed loop is equal to μ<sub>0</sub> times the conduction current passing through the surface.
Consider a charging parallel-plate capacitor: applying Ampere's law to two different surfaces bounded by the same loop yields contradictory results.
Surface S<sub>1</sub> intersects the wire (passing conduction current i), while surface S<sub>2</sub> passes between the capacitor plates (where conduction current is zero).

concept_notes.heading: Introduction of Displacement Current
bullets: To resolve the discontinuity, Maxwell postulated the existence of an additional current due to changing electric flux, termed displacement current i<sub>d</sub>.
It is mathematically expressed as i<sub>d</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> (d&Phi;<sub>E</sub>/dt).
Displacement current does not involve actual movement of charge carriers; rather, it is associated with the time-varying electric field or polarization in a dielectric.

concept_notes.heading: Modified Ampere-Maxwell Law
bullets: The total current enclosed by a loop is the sum of conduction current (i<sub>c</sub>) and displacement current (i<sub>d</sub>).
The modified Ampere's law in integral form is ∮ B · dl = μ<sub>0</sub> (i<sub>c</sub> + ε<sub>0</sub> d&Phi;<sub>E</sub>/dt).
In differential form, it is written as ∇ × B = μ<sub>0</sub> J + μ<sub>0</sub>ε<sub>0</sub> (&partial;E / &partial;t).

concept_notes.heading: Physical Significance and Continuity
bullets: Displacement current ensures the continuity of current through a capacitor; when conduction current drops to zero inside the plates, displacement current takes its exact value.
It is the source of magnetic fields in regions devoid of free charges or conduction currents, such as in empty space for propagating electromagnetic waves.
The product μ<sub>0</sub>ε<sub>0</sub> is inversely proportional to the square of the speed of light in vacuum (c<sup>2</sup>).

derivations.title: Derivation of Displacement Current in a Charging Capacitor
derivations.conditions: Parallel-plate capacitor connected to a time-varying current source
steps: Let the charge on the capacitor plates at any instant t be q, and the area of each plate be A.
The electric field E between the plates is given by E = q / (ε<sub>0</sub> A).
The electric flux Φ<sub>E</sub> through the surface between the plates is Φ<sub>E</sub> = E · A = q / ε<sub>0</sub>.
Differentiating both sides with respect to time t gives dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt = (1 / ε<sub>0</sub>) (dq/dt).
Since dq/dt = i<sub>c</sub> (conduction current), we obtain ε<sub>0</sub> (dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt) = i<sub>c</sub>, which defines the magnitude of the displacement current i<sub>d</sub>.

derivations.title: Modification of Ampere's Circuital Law
derivations.conditions: Time-varying electromagnetic fields in free space or circuits
steps: Take the divergence of the original Ampere's law: ∇ × B = μ<sub>0</sub> J.
Using vector calculus identity, the divergence of a curl is identically zero: ∇ · (∇ × B) = 0.
Therefore, ∇ · J = 0, which contradicts the equation of continuity for time-varying charge distributions: ∇ · J + &partial;ρ/&partial;t = 0.
Substitute ρ using Gauss's law (∇ · E = ρ / ε<sub>0</sub>), giving ∇ · (J + ε<sub>0</sub> &partial;E / &partial;t) = 0.
To make the curl equation consistent with the continuity equation, add the term μ<sub>0</sub>ε<sub>0</sub> (&partial;E / &partial;t) to the right side of Ampere's law.
derivations.result: abla 	imes B = mu_0 J + mu_0 epsilon_0  rac{partial E}{partial t}

formula_sheet.name: Displacement Current Definition
formula_sheet.variables: id = displacement current, ε<sub>0</sub> = permittivity of free space, dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt = rate of change of electric flux

formula_sheet.name: Displacement Current Density
formula_sheet.variables: J<sub>d</sub> = displacement current density, E = electric field vector, t = time

formula_sheet.name: Modified Ampere-Maxwell Law (Integral Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: oint B cdot dl = mu_0 i_c + mu_0 epsilon_0  rac{dPhi_E}{dt}
formula_sheet.variables: B = magnetic field, dl = line element, i<sub>c</sub> = conduction current

formula_sheet.name: Modified Ampere-Maxwell Law (Differential Form)
formula_sheet.equation_html: abla 	imes B = mu_0 J + mu_0 epsilon_0  rac{partial E}{partial t}
formula_sheet.variables: ∇ × B = curl of magnetic field, J = conduction current density

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic Field between Circular Capacitor Plates
formula_sheet.equation_html: B =  rac{mu_0 i r}{2 pi R^2}
formula_sheet.variables: r = radial distance from axis (r < R), R = radius of plates, i = charging current
formula_sheet.conditions: At radius r inside circular parallel-plate capacitor

formula_sheet.name: Electric Flux for Parallel-Plate Capacitor
formula_sheet.variables: Φ<sub>E</sub> = electric flux, q = charge on plate, ε<sub>0</sub> = permittivity

formula_sheet.name: Speed of Electromagnetic Waves
formula_sheet.variables: c = speed of light in vacuum, μ<sub>0</sub> = permeability, ε<sub>0</sub> = permittivity

formula_sheet.name: Total Enclosed Current
formula_sheet.variables: I<sub>total</sub> = total effective current producing magnetic field
formula_sheet.conditions: Any arbitrary surface bounded by a closed loop

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Field vs. Radial Distance in a Charging Capacitor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear increase of B with radius r for r < R, followed by an inverse proportionality (1/r) decrease for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Inside the capacitor plates, displacement current is distributed uniformly across the area, causing B to grow linearly with r. Outside, all displacement/conduction current is effectively concentrated on the axis, leading to 1/r decay.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT numericals and conceptual graphs regarding field profiles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Conduction vs. Displacement Current in an AC Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal wave plot where conduction current in the connecting wires matches the displacement current across the capacitor gap in both amplitude and phase continuity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that displacement current seamlessly continues conduction current across discontinuities like dielectric gaps or capacitors in alternating circuits.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual verification questions in TGT examinations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell's Symmetry Demonstration setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram showing time-varying electric field generating magnetic field and vice versa, leading to self-sustaining electromagnetic wave propagation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights the dual symmetry introduced by displacement current, completing Faraday's law of induction with Maxwell's correction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Short answer and assertion-reasoning questions in PGT physics.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel-plate capacitor with circular plates of radius 5 cm is being charged at a constant rate such that the electric flux between the plates changes at the rate of 10<sup>6</sup> V·m/s. Calculate the displacement current.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt = 10<sup>6</sup> V·m/s.
Recall the formula for displacement current: i<sub>d</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> (dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt).
Substitute the value of permittivity of free space ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854 × 10<sup>-12</sup> C<sup>2</sup>/N·m<sup>2</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel-plate capacitor having plate area 20 cm<sup>2</sup> and separation 1.0 mm is connected to an AC source of voltage V = 100 sin(1000t) volts. Find the peak displacement current between the plates.
solution_steps: Calculate the capacitance C = ε<sub>0</sub> A / d = (8.854 × 10<sup>-12</sup> × 20 × 10<sup>-4</sup>) / (1 × 10<sup>-3</sup>) = 1.77 × 10<sup>-11</sup> F.
The displacement current equals the conduction current in the circuit: i<sub>d</sub>(t) = C (dV/dt).
Multiply to find peak displacement current: I<sub>0,d</sub> = C × V<sub>0</sub> × ω = 1.77 × 10<sup>-11</sup> × 100 × 1000 = 1.77 × 10<sup>-6</sup> A.

solved_numericals.question: The electric field in a region is given by E = E<sub>0</sub> sin(ωt - kx) j-cap. Find the displacement current density vector J<sub>d</sub> at that point.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for displacement current density: J<sub>d</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> (&partial;E / &partial;t).
Perform partial differentiation of E with respect to time t: &partial;E / &partial;t = ω E<sub>0</sub> cos(ωt - kx) j-cap.
Multiply by ε<sub>0</sub> to obtain the vector J<sub>d</sub>.
solved_numericals.answer: epsilon_0 omega E_0 cos(omega t - kx) hat{j}

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes macroscopic electromagnetism where classical field approximations hold valid without quantum electrodynamic corrections.
Valid for isotropic and homogeneous dielectric media when relative permittivity ε<sub>r</sub> is constant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Displacement current involves the actual physical flow of free electrons across the capacitor gap.
common_misconceptions.correct: Displacement current is due to the time-variation of electric flux or electric field, not moving charge.
common_misconceptions.why: No charge carriers move across the vacuum or dielectric barrier of a properly insulated capacitor.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ampere's Circuital Law is completely incorrect and replaced by Maxwell's law.
common_misconceptions.correct: Ampere's law is a special case valid only for steady conduction currents; Maxwell's modification makes it universally valid.
common_misconceptions.why: When electric fields do not change with time (dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt = 0), the displacement current term vanishes, reducing the equation back to original Ampere's law.

quick_revision: Displacement current i<sub>d</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> (dΦ<sub>E</sub>/dt) bridges the gap in Ampere's law for time-varying electric fields.
Displacement Current Definition: i_d = epsilon_0  rac{dPhi_E}{dt}
Displacement Current Density: J_d = epsilon_0  rac{partial E}{partial t}
